title: Customer announcement (draft): Capacity protection for high-traffic routes + updated 429 semantics
content:
Draft for review (Product + Support + CS). Not final customer copy.

Subject: Upcoming update: capacity protection for high-traffic routes and clearer 429 responses

Hi <Customer name>,

We’re rolling out capacity protections for Redwood Inference’s highest-traffic API routes (including /v1/chat/completions, embeddings, and rerank) to improve reliability during bursts, regional pressure, or other fleet-wide contention.

This update is designed to:
- Keep enterprise traffic stable (better p95/p99 latency and fewer 5xx during load)
- Make throttling behavior more predictable for best-effort traffic
- Provide clearer, actionable 429 responses so client retry behavior is correct

No action is required to maintain functionality, but we recommend reviewing the retry/backoff guidance below to ensure your client handles 429s optimally.

What’s changing

1) Tier-aware capacity protection
When Redwood detects sustained pressure (e.g., elevated queue depth / saturation in a region), we’ll apply tier-aware admission control and request shaping.

Practically, this means:
- Enterprise (and other SLA-backed) traffic will be prioritized to maintain defined SLOs for protected routes.
- Best-effort/self-serve traffic may receive 429 responses earlier and more consistently during high-load windows.

2) Clearer 429 semantics (more consistent reason codes + headers)
Previously, a 429 could reflect different limiting conditions with limited visibility. We’re standardizing 429 payloads/headers so you can distinguish between:
- Rate limiting (short-window request rate)
- Quota exhaustion (longer-window usage caps)
- Overload shedding/admission control (fleet protection during pressure)

This is intended to reduce “mystery throttles” and help you choose the right retry strategy.

3) Optional changes in streaming termination behavior under load
For streaming responses, when a request is rejected due to admission control, you may see the stream terminate earlier with a structured error. We’re standardizing termination semantics so clients can reliably detect and retry when appropriate.

What’s NOT changing
- No API path changes.
- No required SDK upgrades (but we recommend keeping SDKs current for best client behavior).
- No immediate billing/pricing changes as part of this rollout (you may see additional metadata for throttling reasons in logs/telemetry).

Who is impacted
- All Hosted API customers can see the improved 429 schema and headers.
- Capacity protection behavior will be most noticeable on a small set of high-traffic “protected routes” during bursty or high-pressure periods.
- Enterprise customers should see more stable latency and fewer error cascades during incidents/bursts.

Rollout plan
- We are rolling out region-by-region, starting with a canary set of accounts and routes.
- During rollout, you may observe changes in the distribution of 429 responses (more consistent earlier shedding for best-effort traffic during pressure).

If you have contractual requirements or a special workload (e.g., highly bursty traffic, large batch jobs, time-sensitive inference windows), please contact us—there is an escalation path for reviewed exceptions.

How to handle 429 responses (recommended client behavior)

At a glance
- Treat all 429 responses as retriable unless the response explicitly indicates a non-retriable policy for your account (rare).
- Always respect Retry-After when provided.
- Use exponential backoff + jitter.
- Cap concurrent retries to avoid retry storms.

Suggested retry algorithm
- If Retry-After is present, wait that long before retrying.
- Otherwise:
  - Backoff: min(60s, base * 2^attempt) with jitter (e.g., base=250ms)
  - Add random jitter of ±20–30%
  - Stop after N attempts (recommend 5–8 depending on your UX)

If your traffic is user-facing, consider:
- Client-side request shaping (queueing + dropping low-priority work)
- Partial fallbacks (smaller model, cached responses, or delayed non-critical tasks)

429 response schema (standardized)

HTTP status
- 429 Too Many Requests

Response body (example)
- Fields may vary slightly by endpoint, but you can expect these keys when present:

{
  "error": {
    "type": "rate_limit_error",
    "message": "Request was throttled. Please retry with backoff.",
    "code": "overload_shed",
    "param": null
  }
}

Reason codes (error.code)
- quota_exceeded: You exhausted a longer-window quota (e.g., daily/monthly cap)
- rate_limited: You exceeded a short-window rate limit (e.g., requests per second)
- overload_shed: Request was rejected to protect fleet health during sustained pressure
- admission_control: Request was rejected due to active admission control for the route/tier
- concurrency_limited: Too many in-flight requests for the account/route (when applicable)

Notes:
- Your integration should not hardcode a fixed set of codes; treat unknown codes as retriable 429s and log them.
- We will avoid high-cardinality “custom” codes; codes are intended to be stable and supportable.

Headers you may see
- Retry-After: seconds to wait before retry (most authoritative)
- X-Redwood-Throttle-Reason: mirrors the high-level reason (e.g., overload_shed)
- X-Redwood-RateLimit-Limit: current request-rate limit (when applicable)
- X-Redwood-RateLimit-Remaining: remaining budget in the current window (when applicable)
- X-Redwood-RateLimit-Reset: time until window reset (when applicable)
- X-Request-Id (or equivalent): include this in support tickets

Important: header names may vary slightly across proxies; rely primarily on Retry-After + response body code where available.

Best practices to reduce throttling during load
- Use request batching where supported (especially embeddings) to reduce overhead per item.
- Avoid large fan-out patterns (e.g., many parallel completions) without a concurrency cap.
- Prefer consistent concurrency over spiky bursts.
- If you maintain multiple routes, isolate background workloads (e.g., periodic reindexing embeddings) from user-facing traffic.

FAQ (draft)

Q: Are you introducing “priority routing”? Does that mean other traffic gets worse?
A: We’re introducing tier-aware capacity protection so enterprise traffic can maintain defined SLOs during fleet pressure. For best-effort traffic, throttling becomes more predictable (more 429s earlier during pressure rather than degraded latency/5xx for everyone).

Q: Does this change my quota/limits?
A: Your contractual limits don’t change as part of this announcement. What changes is the enforcement behavior under pressure and the clarity of 429 responses.

Q: Will I see more 429s?
A: Some customers may see more 429s during bursts or pressure windows—especially for best-effort tiers—because we will shed earlier to prevent long tail latency and cascading failures.

Q: Can I request higher burst limits?
A: Yes. For enterprise workloads, we can review burst requirements and propose an exception with guardrails. Please share your route(s), expected burst size, and business criticality.

Q: How do I tell if this is quota vs overload?
A: Check the error.code (and X-Redwood-Throttle-Reason / Retry-After). Quota-related 429s typically include reset timing; overload/admission control 429s often include Retry-After and may correlate with regional pressure windows.

Support / escalation
- If you believe you’re being throttled unexpectedly (or enterprise traffic is impacted), open a ticket and include:
  - X-Request-Id values for examples
  - Timestamp range + region
  - Endpoint/route + model
  - Observed 429 code(s) + Retry-After behavior
- Enterprise escalation path: contact your TAM/CSM or email <enterprise-support@redwoodinference.example>.

Internal notes (remove before sending)
- Keep customer-facing framing as “capacity protection” / “reliability improvements” rather than “priority routing” unless explicitly requested by enterprise procurement.
- Confirm final header names with Gateway team before finalizing copy.
- Confirm list of protected routes for GA (currently: chat completions, embeddings, rerank; may expand).
- Confirm whether to include concrete SLO numbers per tier (likely “available on request / in your SLA”).
